lessons.title: Functions of Families
lessons.description: What do families do? Parsons, Murdock, feminist and Marxist perspectives on the functions of families.
lessons.content_html:
What Are the Functions of Families?

Sociologists disagree about what families are for and who benefits from them. Where functionalists argue that the family performs essential tasks that hold society together, Marxists argue that the family primarily serves the interests of capitalism, and feminists argue that the family primarily serves the interests of men. Understanding these competing perspectives is essential for your exam.

Murdock’s Four Universal Functions

George Peter Murdock studied 250 societies worldwide and concluded, in his 1949 study Social Structure, that the nuclear family is universal — found in every known human society. He identified four functions that the family performs:

  • Sexual: the family provides a socially approved context for sexual relations between adults, reducing social disruption from unregulated sexuality.
  • Reproductive: the family produces the next generation of society’s members, ensuring biological and social continuity.
  • Economic: the family provides for the material needs of its members — food, shelter, and financial support.
  • Educational: the family transmits culture, norms and values to children through primary socialisation.
Key Fact

Murdock argued that the nuclear family is universal across all 250 societies he studied and performs four essential functions: sexual, reproductive, economic and educational. Functionalists use this evidence to support the view that the family is a necessary institution in every society.

Parsons: Primary Socialisation and Stabilisation

Talcott Parsons extended the functionalist analysis of the family, arguing that in modern industrial societies the family performs two irreducible functions. First, it is responsible for the primary socialisation of children — instilling the shared norms and values that allow individuals to participate in society. Second, it provides the stabilisation of adult personalities. Parsons described this as the “warm bath” effect: the family provides emotional comfort and psychological stability for adult members, releasing the tensions that accumulate in the competitive world of paid work.

Parsons also argued that the instrumental role (performed by the husband/father) and the expressive role (performed by the wife/mother) were biologically grounded and functionally necessary. The instrumental role centres on economic provision; the expressive role centres on emotional nurturing and child rearing. Parsons presented this division as complementary and beneficial to both the family and society.

The functionalist perspective, associated with Murdock and Parsons, argues that the family is a positive institution that meets both individual and societal needs. Murdock saw its four functions as universal necessities. Parsons argued that in modern industrial society, the family has shed many earlier economic and welfare functions (taken over by the state and the economy) but retains the two “irreducible” functions of primary socialisation and personality stabilisation. From this perspective, the nuclear family with its gender-divided roles is the most efficient unit for meeting these needs.

Feminist Critique of Family Functions

Feminist sociologists challenge the functionalist picture fundamentally. Rather than the family performing functions that benefit all members equally, feminists argue that the family primarily benefits men at the expense of women. Ann Oakley argued that the conventional family — with its gendered division of labour — is not a natural arrangement but a socially constructed one that disadvantages women. From Oakley’s perspective, what Parsons called the “expressive role” is in practice unpaid domestic labour that women perform while men benefit from the financial returns of the “instrumental role”.

Delphy and Leonard’s feminist analysis went further, arguing that the family is a patriarchal economic institution. They contended that women’s work within the family — cooking, cleaning, child rearing, emotional support — is systematically exploited by men, who are the primary beneficiaries of this unpaid labour. What Murdock called the “economic function” is, from a feminist view, an arrangement that keeps women economically dependent.

Marxist Critique of Family Functions

Marxist sociologists argue that the family performs an ideological function for capitalism rather than for society as a whole. Eli Zaretsky (1976) argued that the family under capitalism serves two purposes for the bourgeoisie: it reproduces the labour force (workers raise the next generation of workers at their own expense) and it acts as an emotional refuge from the exploitation of capitalist work — meaning that workers’ frustrations are directed at the family rather than at the capitalist system. What Parsons celebrated as the “warm bath” effect, Zaretsky analysed as a mechanism that stabilises capitalism by absorbing workers’ discontent.

From a Marxist perspective, the family also functions as a unit of consumption, purchasing the goods and services that generate profit for the bourgeoisie. Engels, writing in the nineteenth century, argued that the monogamous family arose historically to allow men to identify and pass on their private property to biological heirs — linking the family’s reproductive function directly to the needs of capitalism.

A common error is treating “functions of the family” as a neutral list that all perspectives accept. In fact, while Murdock and Parsons describe the functions positively (the family meets real social needs), Marxists and feminists question whose needs are being served. Feminists point out that describing the mother’s role as “expressive” disguises the fact that it involves substantial unpaid labour. Marxists point out that the family’s “economic function” involves reproducing the workforce and consuming capitalist products. The same activities can be described very differently depending on your theoretical starting point.

Key Fact

Three perspectives compete on family functions: functionalists (Murdock, Parsons) see the family as meeting essential social needs; feminists (Oakley, Delphy and Leonard) see it as serving men’s interests through women’s unpaid labour; Marxists (Zaretsky, Engels) see it as serving capitalism by reproducing the workforce and absorbing worker discontent.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 12-mark Discuss question about family functions, the most common mistake is giving a one-sided answer — listing what functionalists say and stopping there. The mark scheme rewards candidates who present the functionalist view (Murdock’s four functions, Parsons’s two irreducible functions) AND the challenges to it from at least one other perspective (feminist critique of the expressive/instrumental role division, or Zaretsky’s Marxist critique). Name your theorists: “Parsons argued that…” and “Oakley, however, contended that…”. Always end with a supported judgement: explain which perspective you find most convincing and why, using evidence. On a 2-mark Define question, give a definition in sociological language — for “primary socialisation”, write “the earliest stage of socialisation occurring within the family, through which children learn the basic norms and values of their culture”, not just “learning things as a child”.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Murdock identified four universal functions of the family (sexual, reproductive, economic and educational); Parsons argued that in modern industrial society the two irreducible functions are primary socialisation and stabilisation of adult personalities (“warm bath” theory).
  • Feminist sociologists (Oakley; Delphy and Leonard) challenge the functionalist view, arguing that the family’s functions primarily benefit men — the “expressive role” is unpaid female labour; the division of labour is patriarchal, not complementary.
  • Marxist sociologists (Zaretsky; Engels) argue that the family serves the interests of capitalism by reproducing the labour force, absorbing worker discontent and functioning as a unit of consumption for the bourgeoisie.

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): The response presents a sustained, two-sided argument. It covers the functionalist case (Murdock's four universal functions; Parsons's primary socialisation and warm bath theory, expressive and instrumental roles) AND challenges from at least two contrasting perspectives (feminist — Oakley's critique of the expressive/instrumental division as unpaid female labour; Delphy and Leonard's argument that the family exploits women's domestic work for men's benefit; Marxist — Zaretsky's argument that the family serves capitalism by reproducing the workforce and absorbing worker discontent; Engels on the family and private property). At least two named sociologists are developed in detail. Sociological vocabulary is used accurately throughout (primary socialisation, expressive role, patriarchy, bourgeoisie, ideological function). The conclusion weighs the evidence and reaches a substantiated judgement — e.g. identifying that the extent of agreement depends on which perspective is adopted, with evidence.

Secure (7–9 marks): Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced. The judgement is present but development may be uneven — for example, the functionalist case is well developed but the feminist or Marxist challenge is only briefly described.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped on both sides. Some named theorists referenced. Conclusion is present but assertive rather than substantiated.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points, mostly description rather than evaluation. Few or no named sociologists. Little or no judgement.

lessons.title: Family Forms and Family Diversity
lessons.description: Nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent and single sex families. The Rapoports on five types of family diversity.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Family?

There is no single, universally agreed definition of a family in sociology. Rather than adopting one definition as correct, sociologists study the variety of household and kinship arrangements that people live in and the social meanings attached to them. The UK is home to a range of family diversity — different family forms that have become increasingly common since the mid-twentieth century. Understanding each form factually, without privileging one as “normal”, is a key sociological skill.

Major Family Forms in the UK

The following family forms are identified and studied by sociologists:

  • Nuclear family: two parents and their dependent children living together as a self-contained unit. Functionalists such as Parsons argued this is the most efficient family form for modern industrial society.
  • Extended family: a family network that extends beyond the nuclear unit to include grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins. Extended families may be vertically extended (three or more generations) or horizontally extended (relatives of the same generation).
  • Reconstituted family: also called a blended family, formed when two adults — at least one of whom has children from a previous relationship — form a new household together. Reconstituted families have grown in number as divorce rates have risen and remarriage or repartnering has become more common.
  • Lone parent family: one parent living with and responsible for dependent children. ONS data shows that around one in four families with dependent children in the UK is a lone parent family. The majority of lone parents are women.
  • Single sex (same-sex) family: a family in which both parents are of the same sex, including same-sex couples raising children. The Civil Partnership Act 2004 and Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 gave same-sex couples in the UK formal legal recognition.
  • Cohabiting family: a couple (same-sex or different-sex) living together without being married or in a civil partnership, who may or may not have children. Cohabitation has grown significantly in the UK since the 1970s.
Key Fact

The AQA specification identifies five family forms: nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent and single sex. Each describes a different household arrangement. Sociologists study all of them as legitimate family forms without privileging one as the correct or normal version.

Global Family Forms

The spec notes that family forms differ not only within the UK but within a global context. Key examples include:

  • Kibbutz: a collective settlement in which property and sometimes child rearing are shared among the community as a whole. The kibbutz challenged the assumption that child rearing is always a private family function.
  • Polygamy: marriage to more than one spouse simultaneously. Polygyny (one man, multiple wives) is practised in some societies; polyandry (one woman, multiple husbands) is rare. Both are illegal in the UK.

The Rapoports: Five Types of Family Diversity

Rhona and Robert Rapoport argued that British society is characterised by diversity rather than a single dominant family form. Rather than simply counting different family structures, they identified five distinct dimensions of family diversity in their 1982 analysis:

  • Organisational diversity: differences in the way families divide paid and unpaid work. For example, dual-career families versus families with a traditional breadwinner-homemaker split.
  • Cultural diversity: differences related to ethnicity and religion. For example, South Asian families in the UK may have stronger extended kinship networks than White British families; Muslim, Hindu or Jewish families may organise family life differently in relation to gender roles and marriage practices.
  • Social class diversity: working-class and middle-class families differ in income, housing, parenting styles and the opportunities available to children.
  • Life cycle diversity: family structure changes across an individual’s life — a young childless couple, a family with young children, an empty nest family and a widowed individual are all at different life cycle stages.
  • Cohort diversity: people born in different generations have experienced different historical conditions — attitudes to divorce, cohabitation and same-sex partnerships differ markedly between older and younger cohorts.

Not all sociologists regard the growth of family diversity as equally welcome. The New Right, associated with sociologists such as Charles Murray, views the growth of lone parent families and cohabitation with concern, arguing that the breakdown of the traditional nuclear family is linked to a range of social problems including poverty, crime and educational underachievement. Murray argued that lone parent households contribute to a dependency culture and an “underclass”.

Feminist sociologists, by contrast, tend to view the growth of family diversity as reflecting women’s greater economic independence and freedom to leave unhappy marriages and partnerships. From a feminist perspective, the decline of the traditional nuclear family represents progress rather than crisis. Postmodernist sociologists argue that diversity and individual choice are defining features of contemporary life and that no single family form can be presented as superior to others.

Key Fact

The Rapoports (1982) identified five types of family diversity in Britain: organisational, cultural, social class, life cycle and cohort. These show that the family is not a single fixed institution but varies across time, culture and circumstance.

Students sometimes write that “the nuclear family is dying out.” This is an overstatement. ONS data consistently shows that the nuclear family (married or cohabiting couple with dependent children) remains the most common family form in the UK. What has changed is that other family forms have grown in proportion — particularly lone parent families and cohabiting couples. The sociological point is not that the nuclear family has disappeared but that it is no longer the only family form encountered by the majority of the population. The Rapoports’ five types of diversity capture the complexity better than a simple “nuclear family is declining” claim.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark Identify and Describe question about family forms, identify the specific family form clearly (1 mark) and then develop your description with at least two additional points (2 marks). For example: “A reconstituted family is formed when two adults, at least one of whom has children from a previous relationship, form a new household. It is also called a blended family and has become more common as divorce rates have risen.” This answer identifies (reconstituted), describes the defining feature (one or both adults has children from a previous relationship), adds a synonym and links to a social trend — earning all three marks. A common mistake is identifying the family form in one sentence and stopping there, earning only 1 mark. On a 12-mark Discuss about family diversity, never assert that one family form is better or worse than another — present the New Right, feminist and postmodernist views as competing perspectives and let your conclusion weigh the evidence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The AQA specification identifies five family forms: nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent and single sex. The UK also contains cohabiting families, and global examples include the kibbutz and polygamous family forms.
  • The Rapoports (1982) identified five types of family diversity in Britain: organisational, cultural, social class, life cycle and cohort — showing that family diversity runs deeper than simply counting different household structures.
  • Perspectives on family diversity differ: New Right sociologists (Murray) view the growth of lone parent families with concern; feminist sociologists see it as reflecting women's greater independence; postmodernist sociologists celebrate diversity and individual choice as defining features of contemporary life.

lessons.title: Conjugal Role Relationships
lessons.description: Joint and segregated conjugal roles, the domestic division of labour, and Oakley's feminist critique.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Conjugal Roles?

Conjugal roles refer to the roles performed by each partner within a couple relationship. Sociologists distinguish between two broad patterns. Joint conjugal roles (also called integrated conjugal roles) describe partnerships where tasks, decision making and leisure are shared between partners. Segregated conjugal roles describe partnerships where male and female partners have clearly defined separate tasks — typically, the man in paid employment and the woman in domestic work and child rearing. Understanding how sociologists explain these patterns — and whether they are changing — is a key part of the families topic.

The Domestic Division of Labour

The domestic division of labour refers to how unpaid household tasks and child rearing are distributed within the home. Sociologists study a range of activities: cooking, cleaning, laundry, child care, disciplining children, managing household finances, arranging leisure activities and making major household decisions. The central question is whether this division is equal between partners, and whether it has become more equal over time.

Functionalist View: Complementary Roles

Talcott Parsons argued that the gender-divided conjugal role pattern — the man performing the instrumental role (breadwinner, financial provider) and the woman performing the expressive role (homemaker, emotional carer) — was both naturally grounded and functionally efficient. From this perspective, segregated conjugal roles are complementary: each partner contributes different but equally important tasks, and the division benefits the family as a whole. Parsons presented this pattern as meeting the needs of modern industrial society, where paid employment is geographically mobile and requires one adult to be free to move while the other maintains the home.

Peter Willmott and Michael Young (1973) argued that conjugal roles were becoming more equal over time. Their research suggested that the family was moving through historical stages and that the modern family was becoming “symmetrical” — meaning that partners were increasingly sharing domestic tasks and leisure. Willmott and Young described the symmetrical family as one where roles are not identical but broadly equal in the time and effort each partner contributes. They linked this change to the principle of stratified diffusion: lifestyle changes begin among middle-class families and gradually spread to working-class families. For Willmott and Young, the trend towards symmetry was a positive “march of progress” in family life.

Oakley’s Feminist Critique: The Myth of the Symmetrical Family

Ann Oakley directly challenged Willmott and Young’s optimistic picture. Her research on housework, published in The Sociology of Housework (1974), found that the domestic division of labour remained profoundly unequal despite changes in women’s employment. Oakley argued that the conventional family — with its gender-divided roles — was not disappearing but persisting in new forms. She criticised Willmott and Young’s methodology, noting that their data on male domestic participation was based on a very low threshold — men who helped with housework at least once a week counted as “participating.”

Oakley developed the concept of the double shift to describe the burden on women who work in paid employment but continue to perform the majority of domestic labour at home. Rather than replacing domestic work, women’s entry into the paid labour market added a second shift to their day. Some feminist sociologists have extended this to the concept of the triple shift — paid work, domestic labour, and the emotional management of family relationships — to capture the full range of work that women typically carry out.

Key Fact

Willmott and Young (1973) argued that conjugal roles were becoming more equal through the “symmetrical family” and the principle of stratified diffusion. Oakley argued this was a myth — her research showed that the domestic division of labour remained unequal and that women performed a “double shift” of paid work and domestic labour.

Contemporary Issues in Conjugal Roles

Sociologists study a range of contemporary issues that affect the division of roles within couples. Decision making — who has the final say on major financial or household decisions — remains gendered in many households, with research suggesting men retain greater power over major financial decisions. Money management patterns vary: in some families one partner controls all finances; in others both have independent access to income. Dual career families — where both partners are in full-time paid employment — have grown significantly, raising questions about how domestic labour is redistributed. Child rearing responsibilities, including who attends medical appointments, manages schooling and provides primary emotional care, continue to fall disproportionately on women in many families. Leisure activities — how much free time each partner has and how it is used — also differ: research consistently shows that men have more free leisure time than women in couples.

Key Fact

Feminist sociologists argue that the domestic division of labour remains unequal in contemporary British families. Women who work full-time still perform more domestic labour and child care than their male partners on average, supporting Oakley’s concept of the double shift.

From a Marxist perspective, the domestic division of labour serves the interests of capitalism as well as men. The unpaid domestic labour of women — cooking, cleaning, child rearing, caring for sick and elderly family members — reproduces the labour force at no cost to employers. This work is economically invisible: it does not appear in GDP or in wage statistics, yet it sustains the workforce. Marxist feminists argue that the conventional family therefore benefits the bourgeoisie as well as individual men, because it means the costs of reproducing workers across generations are borne by families rather than by the state or employers.

Key Takeaways

  • Conjugal roles describe how partners divide paid work, domestic tasks and child rearing. Joint conjugal roles are relatively equal; segregated conjugal roles assign distinct tasks by gender. The domestic division of labour covers decision making, money management, child rearing, domestic tasks and leisure.
  • Willmott and Young (1973) argued the family was becoming symmetrical through the principle of stratified diffusion. Oakley challenged this as a myth — her research showed the domestic division of labour remained unequal and women performed a double shift of paid work and domestic labour.
  • Parsons (functionalist) saw gender-divided conjugal roles as complementary and beneficial. Marxists argue that women's unpaid domestic labour reproduces the workforce at no cost to capitalism. Feminists (Oakley) argue the conventional family is a patriarchal institution that exploits women's labour.

lessons.title: Changing Relationships Within Families
lessons.description: Willmott and Young's symmetrical family, stratified diffusion, and contemporary family issues.
lessons.content_html:
How Have Families Changed Over Time?

Sociologists examine how family relationships have changed across three broad historical periods: pre-industrial, industrial and contemporary. Understanding this historical trajectory — and the competing perspectives on whether change has been progressive or problematic — is central to the families topic. Different perspectives offer strikingly different evaluations of the same changes.

The Pre-Industrial Family

In pre-industrial Britain (before approximately the mid-eighteenth century), the family was primarily a unit of economic production. Most families worked together in agriculture or craft production. The household typically included not just parents and children but also servants, apprentices and extended kin. The boundary between work and home was blurred; family members of all ages contributed economically. Peter Laslett’s historical research challenged the idea that the pre-industrial family was predominantly an extended unit, finding that nuclear family households were more common than often assumed. However, extended kinship networks of support remained significant even if not co-resident.

The Industrial Family

Industrialisation (roughly 1750–1900) transformed the family. Paid work moved out of the home and into factories and offices. This created a sharper separation between the public sphere (paid work) and the private sphere (the home). The nuclear family became the dominant household form, with a clear gender division: the man in paid employment, the woman managing the home. Working-class families often had both adults and children in paid work in early industrialisation, but as the nineteenth century progressed, middle-class values of the male breadwinner and the “domestic wife” spread downward through the principle of stratified diffusion. The family shifted from a unit of production to a unit of consumption.

Willmott and Young: Towards the Symmetrical Family

Peter Willmott and Michael Young (1973) developed an influential account of the contemporary family in their study The Symmetrical Family. They argued that the family had passed through three historical stages and was now entering a fourth, characterised by the symmetrical family. In this form, both partners are likely to be in paid employment, both participate in domestic tasks and child rearing, and both have leisure time together. Willmott and Young saw this as a positive “march of progress.”

Central to their explanation was the principle of stratified diffusion. They observed that the symmetrical family pattern appeared first among middle-class households and was gradually spreading to the working class as material conditions improved. Higher incomes, better housing and the growth of home-centred leisure (television, home ownership) all contributed to what Willmott and Young called privatised instrumentalism — families becoming increasingly self-contained and home-focused.

Key Fact

Willmott and Young (1973) argued that the family was becoming “symmetrical” — roles more equally shared — and that this change spread from middle-class to working-class families through the principle of stratified diffusion. They presented this as a positive historical progression.

Ann Oakley challenged Willmott and Young directly, arguing that the “march of progress” narrative was misleading. Her research found that the domestic division of labour remained highly unequal: women still performed the vast majority of domestic tasks and child care, even when in full-time paid employment. Oakley criticised the low threshold used by Willmott and Young to define male domestic participation. From her feminist perspective, the symmetrical family was a myth that served to obscure continuing gender inequality in the home.

From a Marxist perspective, the “march of progress” in family life is better understood as a change in the form of family serving capitalism rather than as genuine liberation. Higher wages and consumerism drew the working-class family into the home-centred, high-consumption lifestyle that generates profit for the bourgeoisie. Privatised instrumentalism, far from representing freedom, ties families more closely to consumption patterns that benefit capitalism.

Contemporary Family Issues

The spec identifies several contemporary family issues that sociologists study. These reflect the ways in which family relationships continue to evolve and the challenges that arise from changing social conditions:

  • Quality of parenting: sociologists debate whether parenting standards are changing. Some argue that greater awareness of child development and increased investment of time and resources in children has improved parenting; others point to the pressures of long working hours, poverty and social media as creating new challenges. Perspectives differ on what “good parenting” means and who defines it.
  • Relationships between teenagers and adults: the concept of adolescence as a distinct life stage is itself a modern, socially constructed category. Sociologists note that the extension of education and financial dependence on parents has prolonged adolescence. Intergenerational tensions within families are studied as social phenomena rather than as natural or inevitable.
  • Care of disabled and elderly family members: as life expectancy has increased, the issue of who cares for elderly or disabled family members has grown. Feminist sociologists note that caring responsibilities fall disproportionately on women. The state provides some care services, but much informal care is provided by female relatives.
  • Arranged marriage: sociologists distinguish between arranged marriage (where families identify suitable partners but individuals give their consent) and forced marriage (where individuals are compelled to marry against their will, which is illegal in the UK). Arranged marriage is practised in various communities in the UK and globally and is not inherently coercive; sociologists study it without imposing a single moral judgement.
Key Fact

The spec requires knowledge of contemporary family issues including quality of parenting, teenager–adult relationships, care of the disabled and elderly, and arranged marriage. Sociologists study each of these as social phenomena shaped by wider structural factors — not as simply individual or natural.

From a functionalist perspective, changes in family relationships across history represent the family adapting to meet the changing needs of society. As the economy shifted from agriculture to industry to post-industrial service work, the family shed functions it could no longer efficiently perform (transferred to schools, hospitals and the state) and retained those it was best placed to deliver — primary socialisation and personality stabilisation. Willmott and Young’s symmetrical family thesis can be read as a functionalist account: the family evolves to meet the needs of a more egalitarian society. Critics of the functionalist view, however, argue that it presents change as evolutionary and benign while obscuring the structural inequalities that shape family life.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Describe question about Willmott and Young, name them directly and describe both their key concept (the symmetrical family) and their explanation of how change occurs (the principle of stratified diffusion). A common mistake is describing the symmetrical family without explaining the mechanism — you need both for 4 marks. On the 12-mark Discuss, a strong response on changing family relationships must present the “march of progress” argument (Willmott and Young) alongside its critics (Oakley’s feminist critique; Marxist critique) and reach a supported judgement. Avoid treating Willmott and Young’s thesis as fact — present it as one perspective and then evaluate it using Oakley’s counter-evidence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Families have changed across three historical periods: pre-industrial (family as unit of production), industrial (separation of work and home, male breadwinner/female homemaker), and contemporary (growth of dual career families, greater role sharing, privatisation of family life).
  • Willmott and Young (1973) argued the modern family was becoming symmetrical, with roles more equally shared, driven by the principle of stratified diffusion from middle to working class. Oakley challenged this as a myth — her research showed women still performed the majority of domestic labour.
  • Contemporary family issues studied by sociologists include quality of parenting, teenager–adult relationships, care of disabled and elderly family members, and arranged marriage. Each is shaped by structural factors including gender, class, ethnicity and state policy.

lessons.title: Criticisms of Families
lessons.description: Isolation, idealisation and marital breakdown. Zaretsky's Marxist and Delphy and Leonard's feminist critiques.
lessons.content_html:
Why Are Families Criticised?

While functionalist sociologists emphasise the positive functions that families perform, a range of other perspectives offer sustained critiques of family life. These critiques come from different directions: feminist and Marxist sociologists identify structural problems with the family as an institution, while other critics point to the gap between the idealised image of family life and its lived reality. Understanding these criticisms — and the competing perspectives behind them — is central to the AQA families topic.

The Problem of Isolation

One criticism of the modern nuclear family is that it has become socially isolated. As the nuclear family has become more self-contained and home-centred (what Willmott and Young called “privatised”), it has lost contact with extended kinship networks and local communities. This isolation can place enormous pressure on individual family members, particularly when problems arise: there is no wider network to absorb the stress. Critics argue that the isolated nuclear family is an emotionally intense unit that can generate conflict, mental health problems and domestic violence, rather than automatically providing the “warm bath” effect that Parsons described.

Unrealistic Idealisation and Loss of Traditional Functions

A related criticism is the idealisation of family life. Advertising, popular culture and political discourse consistently portray the family as a place of unconditional love and support. Critics argue that this idealised image conceals the very real conflicts, inequalities and abuses that occur within families. Domestic violence, emotional abuse, child neglect and financial exploitation are all more likely to occur within family settings than between strangers — yet these realities are underrepresented in public discourse about family life.

Sociologists also note the loss of traditional functions from the family. Functions once performed within the family — economic production, religious instruction, health care, education — have been transferred to external institutions (schools, hospitals, the state, employers). Parsons acknowledged this and argued that the family adapted by specialising in primary socialisation and personality stabilisation. Critics, however, argue that this “loss of functions” has left some families without a clear sense of purpose and has reduced the family’s capacity to support its members in practical ways.

Dysfunctional families are those in which relationships cause harm rather than provide support. Sociologists use the term to describe families characterised by persistent conflict, domestic violence, substance abuse, neglect or emotional harm. The New Right argues that growing family diversity — particularly the growth of lone parent families and cohabitation — has increased the prevalence of dysfunctional families and associated social problems. Feminist sociologists challenge this, arguing that the concept of “dysfunctional family” is often used to pathologise lone parent families without recognising the structural causes of their difficulties (poverty, lack of affordable child care, the gender pay gap).

Marital breakdown is a related concern. This can take the form of legal divorce, long-term separation, or an empty shell marriage — a marriage that continues legally but in which the partners have effectively ceased to have a meaningful relationship. Sociologists distinguish between marital breakdown and divorce: not all unhappy marriages end in divorce, and not all divorces indicate relationship failure (some reflect changing legal and social norms).

The Status and Role of Women Within Families: Feminist Critiques

Feminist sociologists have been among the most influential critics of the family as an institution. Rather than viewing the family as a haven, they identify it as a site of patriarchy. Two key feminist accounts are particularly important for the AQA specification.

Ann Oakley argued that the role of women within families has been constructed around the expectation of unpaid domestic service. Women’s labour in the home — cooking, cleaning, child care, emotional management — is treated as natural and invisible rather than as skilled work with economic value. The conventional family, Oakley argued, is not a partnership of equals but a system in which women’s time and labour are taken for granted.

Delphy and Leonard developed a more explicitly structural feminist critique in their work. They argued that the family is best understood as a patriarchal family — an economic institution in which the husband is the head and the primary beneficiary of all the work performed within the household. Delphy and Leonard argued that women’s domestic labour is a form of economic exploitation: women produce services and care for which they receive little or no financial compensation. This is not a matter of individual men being selfish but of a structural arrangement in which men as a group systematically benefit from women’s unpaid work in the family.

Key Fact

Two major critical perspectives on the family are: Zaretsky’s Marxist critique (the family serves capitalism by reproducing the labour force and absorbing worker discontent) and Delphy and Leonard’s feminist critique (the family is a patriarchal economic institution in which women’s domestic labour is exploited for men’s benefit).

Zaretsky’s Marxist Critique

Eli Zaretsky (1976) offered a Marxist account of the development of the family under capitalism. He argued that as industrial capitalism separated work from home in the nineteenth century, the family came to be presented as a private refuge from the public world of economic exploitation. But Zaretsky argued that this was an ideological function: the family does not actually provide freedom from capitalism but instead naturalises and reproduces capitalist social relations. Workers who experience alienation and exploitation at work are directed to seek fulfilment in family life — reducing the likelihood of collective resistance to capitalism.

Zaretsky also argued that the family functions as a unit of consumption, purchasing the commodities produced by capitalist industry. The home — filled with appliances, food, clothing and entertainment — is a major market for capitalist goods. From this perspective, the celebration of home and family life in consumer culture serves the interests of the bourgeoisie rather than genuinely meeting workers’ needs.

Key Fact

Delphy and Leonard argued the family is a patriarchal economic institution exploiting women’s unpaid labour. Zaretsky argued the family serves capitalism by absorbing worker discontent and acting as a unit of consumption.

Functionalists respond to these criticisms by arguing that critics focus on the dysfunctions of family life while undervaluing its genuine benefits. Murdock and Parsons maintained that the family performs necessary functions — particularly primary socialisation and personality stabilisation — that no other institution performs as effectively. While dysfunctional families clearly exist, functionalists argue that these represent failures of the institution rather than evidence against the institution itself. Parsons acknowledged that the isolated nuclear family could be emotionally intense, but argued that this intensity was the price of the deep emotional bonds that make effective primary socialisation possible.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Describe question about Zaretsky or Delphy and Leonard, always name the sociologist and state both their general argument AND a specific mechanism. For Zaretsky: (1) the family absorbs worker discontent (keeping capitalism stable) and (2) acts as a unit of consumption (benefiting the bourgeoisie). For Delphy and Leonard: (1) the family is a patriarchal economic institution and (2) women’s domestic labour is exploited for men’s benefit. Describing only one mechanism usually earns 2 marks; both mechanisms with the sociologist named earns 4. On the 12-mark Discuss about criticisms of families, present the feminist critique (Oakley; Delphy and Leonard), the Marxist critique (Zaretsky) and the functionalist defence (Murdock, Parsons) as three competing perspectives, then reach a supported judgement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Criticisms of families include: social isolation of the nuclear family; unrealistic idealisation concealing conflict and abuse; loss of traditional functions; dysfunctional families; marital breakdown; empty shell marriages; and the inferior status and role of women within families.
  • Delphy and Leonard's feminist critique identifies the family as a patriarchal economic institution in which women's domestic labour is systematically exploited for men's benefit. Oakley argued that women's role as homemaker is not complementary but exploitative.
  • Zaretsky's Marxist critique argues that the family serves capitalism by absorbing worker discontent (reducing resistance) and functioning as a unit of consumption (generating profit for the bourgeoisie). Both critiques challenge the functionalist view that the family benefits all members equally.

lessons.title: Divorce: Patterns, Causes and Consequences
lessons.description: Rising divorce since 1945: legal change, secularisation and women's independence. Consequences for families.
lessons.content_html:
Divorce in Britain Since 1945

Divorce is the legal ending of a marriage. The pattern of divorce in Britain since 1945 is one of dramatic and sustained increase, followed by a plateau and some decline in more recent years. In the decade after the Second World War, divorce was relatively rare — around 25,000 divorces per year. By the mid-1990s this figure had risen to around 175,000 per year. Since then the rate has declined somewhat, partly because marriage itself has become less common (more couples cohabit rather than marry, so fewer marriages can end in divorce). Understanding the causes and consequences of this change is a central requirement of the AQA families topic.

Reasons for the Rise in Divorce: Legal Changes

One of the most significant causes of the rising divorce rate was legal change. The Divorce Reform Act 1969 came into force in 1971 and fundamentally changed the legal basis of divorce in England and Wales. Before 1969, divorce required proof of a matrimonial “offence” (such as adultery or cruelty). The 1969 Act replaced this with a single ground: irretrievable breakdown of marriage. This made divorce substantially easier and cheaper to obtain, and the divorce rate almost doubled in the years immediately after it came into force. Subsequent legal changes, including the introduction of legal aid for divorce cases, further reduced the practical barriers to obtaining a divorce.

Changing Social Attitudes and Secularisation

Legal change does not occur in a social vacuum. The Divorce Reform Act 1969 reflected — and further accelerated — a broader shift in social attitudes towards divorce. As Britain became an increasingly secularised society, the religious stigma attached to divorce diminished. The Church of England and the Roman Catholic Church had traditionally taught that marriage was a lifelong sacrament and that divorce was morally wrong. As church attendance fell and religious authority over personal life weakened, divorce became more socially acceptable. By the end of the twentieth century, divorce carried little social stigma in most communities.

More broadly, changing social values contributed to higher divorce rates. The growing expectation that marriage should provide personal fulfilment, romantic love and emotional intimacy — rather than simply economic partnership or social respectability — raised the threshold for what was considered a “good enough” marriage. When marriages fell below this standard, individuals were more likely to seek divorce rather than continue in an unhappy relationship. Sociologists describe this as a shift from an “institutional” to a “companionate” model of marriage.

Key Fact

Four main reasons explain the rise in divorce since 1945: (1) legal change — the Divorce Reform Act 1969 introduced irretrievable breakdown as grounds for divorce; (2) secularisation — declining religious stigma against divorce; (3) changing social attitudes and rising expectations of marriage; (4) the changing status of women in society.

The Changing Status of Women

A particularly important cause of rising divorce rates is the changing status of women in society. Women’s increasing participation in paid employment since the Second World War has given many women greater economic independence. This has reduced the financial dependence on a male partner that previously made divorce an unviable option for many women. Research consistently shows that the majority of divorce petitions in Britain are filed by women — suggesting that women are more likely to seek to end unsatisfactory marriages when they have the means to do so.

The changing status of women is also linked to changing expectations: women’s greater social and political equality has raised their expectations of what a marriage should provide. The continued unequal distribution of domestic labour (Oakley’s double shift) means that many women experience marriage as disproportionately burdensome, and rising aspirations make this burden less acceptable over time.

Consequences of Divorce for Family Members

The consequences of divorce affect all members of the family. For husbands and wives, divorce can bring both relief from an unhappy relationship and significant emotional, financial and practical difficulties. Women tend to experience greater financial hardship after divorce (since they are more likely to have reduced their participation in paid employment during the marriage). Men tend to experience greater social isolation after divorce (since they are less likely to have primary care of children and may have weaker social networks).

For children, sociological research presents a complex picture. Some research suggests that parental conflict — not divorce itself — is the key factor in children’s outcomes, meaning that divorce may in some cases be better for children than continuing an acrimonious marriage. Other research highlights the economic and social disadvantages associated with growing up in a lone parent household, including lower educational achievement and poorer health outcomes. Sociologists caution against treating all divorces as equally harmful, since outcomes vary significantly with income, quality of post-divorce parenting arrangements and the degree of continued conflict between former partners.

For the extended family, divorce disrupts grandparent–grandchild relationships and wider kinship networks. Grandparents on the non-resident parent’s side may lose contact with grandchildren. The rise of divorce has also contributed significantly to the growth of lone parent families in the UK, since many divorces involve children.

Serial monogamy describes the practice of having a succession of monogamous relationships or marriages — one at a time rather than simultaneously. As divorce has become more socially acceptable, more people go on to form new partnerships and remarry after divorce. Sociologists argue this reflects not a rejection of marriage as an institution but an individualisation of relationship choice. Some functionalists see serial monogamy as evidence that marriage remains highly valued — people seek it again after it breaks down rather than abandoning the institution.

An empty shell marriage, by contrast, is a marriage that persists legally but in which the couple have effectively separated emotionally, though they remain formally married. Empty shell marriages may persist for financial reasons (e.g. maintaining a joint mortgage), social reasons (e.g. religious objection to divorce) or for the perceived benefit of children. The concept is important because it shows that official divorce statistics undercount the number of relationships that have actually broken down.

Functionalist view: Parsons argued that the family adapts to meet social needs. From this perspective, rising divorce rates do not necessarily signal a “crisis” of the family but may reflect rising expectations of what marriage should provide. High remarriage rates suggest that marriage as an institution remains valued, even if individual marriages fail.

Feminist view: Most divorce petitions are filed by women, supporting the feminist argument that marriage has historically placed greater burdens on women. Rising divorce rates may reflect women’s growing economic independence and their capacity to leave unsatisfactory relationships. From this perspective, divorce is not a symptom of social breakdown but of women’s liberation from patriarchal constraints.

Marxist view: Marxists argue that the causes of marital breakdown are often rooted in the economic conditions of capitalism — poverty, financial stress and the alienation of work all increase pressure on family relationships. The increasing commodification of family life (consumer debt, housing insecurity) generates tensions that contribute to marital breakdown.

New Right view: Murray’s New Right perspective is critical of rising divorce rates, arguing that the growth of lone parent families resulting from divorce contributes to a dependency culture and the development of an underclass. The New Right argues that children raised without two parents are disadvantaged educationally and socially. This view has been challenged by feminist sociologists, who argue it pathologises lone parent families while ignoring the structural causes of their difficulties.

Key Fact

The main consequences of divorce include: financial hardship (particularly for women); social isolation (particularly for men); impacts on children’s educational and health outcomes; disruption of extended family relationships; and a significant increase in the number of lone parent families in the UK.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Describe question about reasons for rising divorce rates, use the four-part structure: legal change (Divorce Reform Act 1969), secularisation (declining religious stigma), changing social attitudes (rising expectations of marriage) and the changing status of women (greater economic independence). One mark per reason is the typical pattern, so covering all four and naming the 1969 Act secures full marks. On the 12-mark Discuss, never present divorce as inherently a social problem — that is the New Right view (Murray), not an authorial claim. Present the New Right view as one perspective alongside the feminist view (rising divorce reflects women’s independence) and the functionalist view (the institution of marriage remains valued despite individual failures). Name your sociologists explicitly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Divorce rates in Britain rose dramatically from the 1970s, driven by legal change (Divorce Reform Act 1969), secularisation, changing social attitudes and the growing economic independence and changing status of women. Since the mid-1990s rates have slightly declined, partly because marriage itself is less common.
  • Consequences of divorce include financial hardship (especially for women), social isolation (especially for men), varied impacts on children's wellbeing, disruption of extended family networks and the significant growth of lone parent families in the UK.
  • Perspectives on divorce differ: functionalists see rising rates as reflecting changing expectations rather than family breakdown; feminists see them as evidence of women's growing independence; Marxists link marital breakdown to economic pressures; the New Right (Murray) views rising divorce and lone parenthood as contributing to an underclass and social problems.

lessons.title: Researching Families
lessons.description: Researching families: surveys, interviews and official statistics. Challenges of studying private family life.
lessons.content_html:
Why Is Researching Families Challenging?

Families are one of the most private social institutions. Unlike schools, workplaces or public spaces, families are largely closed to outside observation. This creates significant practical issues for sociologists who wish to study family life: gaining access, maintaining trust and capturing honest behaviour. At the same time, families involve deeply personal relationships — raising sensitive ethical issues around consent, confidentiality and the potential for harm. AQA requires students to evaluate research methods applied specifically to families, not just in the abstract.

Surveys and Questionnaires: Studying the Domestic Division of Labour

Surveys using questionnaires have been widely used to study the domestic division of labour and conjugal roles. Willmott and Young’s research for The Symmetrical Family (1973) used large-scale surveys to gather data from hundreds of households about how domestic tasks were divided. This quantitative approach allowed them to identify broad patterns and trends across social classes.

However, surveys have important limitations when used to study family life. Questionnaires produce data that is easily comparable and statistically analysable but may lack depth. Respondents may give socially desirable answers — describing a more equal division of tasks than actually exists — rather than recording their genuine behaviour. Ann Oakley criticised this limitation directly in her critique of Willmott and Young: their survey data on male domestic participation was based on a low threshold, and respondents may have overstated male involvement. Qualitative methods may better capture the complexity of domestic life than tick-box questionnaires.

Interviews: Gaining Depth on Family Experience

Oakley’s own research on housework used in-depth interviews with women about their experience of domestic labour. She used unstructured interviews, which allowed participants to speak freely in their own words about their experiences and feelings. This generated rich qualitative data about women’s attitudes to housework, their sense of identity and the emotional demands of domestic labour — data that a survey could not have captured.

Interviews have significant advantages for researching sensitive aspects of family life, such as experiences of domestic violence, parenting practices or the experience of divorce. They allow the researcher to probe for detail, follow up unexpected responses and build rapport with participants. However, they are also time-consuming and expensive, produce data that is difficult to generalise from a small sample, and rely on participants reporting their experiences honestly — which may be particularly problematic for sensitive topics within families.

Key Fact

Willmott and Young used large-scale surveys (quantitative) to study the domestic division of labour — allowing broad patterns to be identified but risking socially desirable responses. Oakley used in-depth unstructured interviews (qualitative) with women about housework — generating rich, detailed data but with a smaller, less generalisable sample.

Observation of Family Life

Observation of family life raises acute practical and ethical challenges. Observing family behaviour in its natural setting — the home — could provide highly valid data about how families actually behave (rather than what they say they do). However, gaining access to private family homes for observation is extremely difficult. Even when access is granted, families are likely to change their behaviour when they know they are being observed, creating a Hawthorne effect.

Participant observation — where the researcher lives with or becomes part of the family for a period — could generate highly naturalistic data, but raises serious ethical issues about intrusion into private life, the boundaries of the researcher’s role, and the potential for family members to feel pressured to participate. The Rapoports’ research on family diversity involved extensive contact with families over time, using a mixed methods approach combining interviews with observational elements.

Official Statistics on Families

Official statistics are a major source of data for studying family patterns. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes annual data on marriage rates, divorce rates, cohabitation, household composition, lone parent families and birth rates. The census collects detailed data on household composition every ten years.

Official statistics on divorce, marriage and family forms are quantitative, nationally representative and freely available, making them highly convenient for sociologists. However, they have significant limitations. Official statistics on families count legal arrangements (married couples, registered civil partnerships, legal divorces) but miss cohabiting couples who separate without legal proceedings and families that do not conform to standard administrative categories. Marriage and divorce statistics also change with legal reform (as the dramatic effect of the Divorce Reform Act 1969 demonstrates) — meaning trends in statistics may partly reflect changes in law rather than changes in family behaviour.

Practical issues include: access — families are private institutions and researchers cannot simply enter without invitation. Recruiting family research participants often requires working through schools, community centres, online networks or snowball sampling. Time and cost — longitudinal studies of families (tracking the same households over years or decades) are expensive and resource-intensive, though they yield valuable data on how families change. Representativeness — families that agree to participate in research may not be typical of all families (those experiencing serious domestic problems, for example, are less likely to volunteer for a study of “family life”). Changing composition — families change over time through births, deaths, divorce, remarriage and children leaving home, making longitudinal family research methodologically complex.

Key Fact

The AQA specification requires students to know three ethical issues in research: consent, confidentiality and harm. In family research, these apply with particular force: family members must all give informed consent; data about family relationships must be kept confidential; and researchers must consider the potential for their presence or questions to cause distress, particularly when studying sensitive topics such as domestic abuse, divorce or child neglect.

Informed consent is particularly complex when researching families with children. Children below the age of consent cannot legally give consent themselves, so parents or guardians must consent on their behalf. However, sociologists debate whether parental consent alone is sufficient — should children also give their assent? Children may feel unable to refuse to participate if their parents have agreed. Confidentiality is also challenging: if a researcher discovers evidence of child abuse or neglect during family research, they face a conflict between their duty of confidentiality to participants and their legal and moral obligation to protect the child from harm. AQA requires students to think about how ethical issues “can be addressed” — not just identified. Possible approaches include: briefing participants clearly about the limits of confidentiality before the study begins; using independent child welfare advisers; ensuring children can speak to researchers separately from parents.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 12-mark Discuss about researching families, the key AQA requirement is to evaluate a method IN CONTEXT — not to recite generic strengths and weaknesses. So don’t just write “observation is time-consuming.” Instead, write: “Participant observation of family life is particularly difficult because the home is a private space and families may change their behaviour significantly when observed — reducing the validity of the data.” Linking the evaluation to the specific challenges of family research earns application marks (AO2). On a 4-mark Describe about official statistics on families, name the ONS and the census, explain what data they provide, and then evaluate: state that they miss cohabiting couples, undercount relationship breakdown and reflect legal change as well as social change.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Surveys (used by Willmott and Young) allow large-scale quantitative data on the domestic division of labour but risk socially desirable responses. Unstructured interviews (used by Oakley) generate rich qualitative data on women's experiences of domestic life but are harder to generalise. Observation of families is valuable in principle but raises acute practical and ethical challenges around access and intrusion.
  • Official statistics (ONS, census) provide nationally representative data on marriage, divorce and family forms, but miss informal cohabiting relationships, undercount relationship breakdown and may reflect legal change rather than social change.
  • Ethical issues in family research include: informed consent (especially where children are involved), confidentiality (and its limits when abuse is discovered) and harm. AQA requires students to explain how these issues can be addressed, not just name them.

Which research method did Ann Oakley use in her study of housework, generating rich qualitative data about women's experiences of domestic labour?
A) Postal questionnaire
B) Official statistics analysis
C) Non-participant observation
D) Unstructured interviews
practice_questions.marks: D) Unstructured interviews [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'informed consent' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that participants are given information about the research; 1 mark for indicating that they make a free and voluntary decision to take part. Example: 'Informed consent means that research participants are given sufficient information about the study — its purpose, methods and how data will be used — to make a free and voluntary decision about whether to take part.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one ethical issue that arises specifically when researching families with children.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an ethical issue (e.g. informed consent with children; confidentiality limits when abuse is discovered; risk of harm to child participants). 2 marks for a developed description including how the issue can be addressed: e.g. 'Children below the age of consent cannot legally give consent themselves, so parents or guardians must consent on their behalf. However, sociologists debate whether parental consent alone is sufficient — children may feel unable to refuse if their parents have agreed. One way to address this is to speak to children separately from their parents, making clear that their participation is voluntary and will not affect their relationship with their parents.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the strengths and weaknesses of using official statistics to study divorce and family change in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for a strength: official statistics are nationally representative and produced annually by the ONS, making them a reliable source for identifying broad trends over time (e.g. rising divorce rates after the 1969 Act). 1 mark for a second strength or detail: they are freely available, cover the entire population (unlike small-scale studies) and are consistent across time, allowing longitudinal comparisons. 1 mark for a weakness: official divorce statistics only count legal divorces and miss informal separations (cohabiting couples who split without legal proceedings) and empty shell marriages — meaning they undercount actual relationship breakdown. 1 mark for a second weakness: divorce statistics partly reflect changes in the law (the Divorce Reform Act 1969 caused an immediate spike in figures) rather than changes in relationship quality or behaviour.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one practical challenge a sociologist would face when using observation to study family life.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a practical challenge (e.g. gaining access to private family homes; the Hawthorne effect; changing family composition; time and cost). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'A major practical challenge is gaining access — families are private institutions and most people would be reluctant to allow a researcher to observe their home life. Even when access is granted, families are likely to behave differently when aware of being observed (the Hawthorne effect), which reduces the validity of the data — the researcher may observe an idealised version of family life rather than everyday behaviour.'

practice_questions.text: "Questionnaires are the best method for sociologists studying family life." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A sustained two-sided argument evaluating questionnaires in the specific context of family research. Arguments in support: Willmott and Young used large-scale surveys successfully to identify patterns in the domestic division of labour — questionnaires are practical, cheap to administer to large samples, produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and allows broad trends to be identified. They can be completed anonymously, reducing embarrassment on sensitive topics. Arguments against: questionnaires risk socially desirable responses — Oakley found that Willmott and Young's survey data overstated male domestic participation because respondents gave the 'right' answer rather than an honest one; questionnaires produce limited depth on complex relationships and emotions; closed questions cannot capture the nuances of family experience. Unstructured interviews (Oakley) generate richer data. Observation could provide more naturalistic data but raises access and ethical problems. Mixed methods offer a solution — combining surveys for breadth with interviews for depth. Named sociologists (Willmott and Young, Oakley) developed in detail. Sociological vocabulary used accurately (quantitative, qualitative, validity, reliability, Hawthorne effect, socially desirable response, informed consent). Supported conclusion.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides of the questionnaire debate present, named sociologists, judgement present.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant points, mainly one-sided or undeveloped.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points, mainly description, little judgement.

glossary_terms.definition: Research that produces numerical data and is concerned with measuring social phenomena across large samples, often using questionnaires or official statistics.
Research that produces rich, descriptive data about people's meanings and experiences, typically through interviews or observation.
The principle that research participants must be given sufficient information about the study to make a free and voluntary decision about whether to take part.
The ethical principle that information shared by research participants will not be disclosed in a way that identifies them without their permission.
A national survey of all households, conducted in the UK every ten years, providing comprehensive demographic data on family forms and household composition.
The extent to which a research method measures what it claims to measure and produces an accurate picture of social reality.
The extent to which a research method produces consistent results when repeated under the same conditions.
Difficulties in carrying out research related to time, cost and access to participants or settings, rather than to ethical concerns.
